extracted.intended_audience: readers of The A.V. Club and fans of satirical comedy (The Onion); general-interest humor readers
extracted.subtask_description: A magazine/feature piece in which staff pick a single Onion article that best defines or represents them and explain why; mixes personal anecdote with commentary on what makes those Onion pieces effective. Useful for understanding what qualities readers/personas find resonant in satirical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal resonance / identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick an Onion article that defined who you are, that you identify with so much that it actually makes you a bit uneasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prompt and multiple staff answers emphasize choosing pieces that feel personally true or revealing (e.g., 'Area Man Really Wants To Like The Marx Brothers', 'Aging Gen-Xer Doesn't Find Bad Movies Funny Anymore'). The piece should evoke a sense of recognition or discomfort in the reader/subject; examples in the article show readers selecting items because they saw themselves in the archetype or behavior portrayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humane, exacting skepticism (not merely cynicism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire should come from a place of humane, exacting skepticism rather than pure cynicism: 'The Onion is pretty short on cynicism. When it hurts, it hurts because it cares.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective Onion pieces critique grand claims and institutions while still showing concern; the best satire here 'cares' about its subjects and critiques promises stitched into belief systems (e.g., 'Glorious New Tomorrow Postponed Indefinitely'). This is a qualitative tonal bar: biting but not nihilistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Makes readers confront the absurdity of personal quirks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onion is at its best when it makes us confront the absurdity of our personal quirks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several staff choices are pieces that highlight petty, obsessive, or embarrassing behaviors ('Report: Guy Just Put 10 Bucks In Jukebox', 'Ironic Porn Purchase Leads To Unironic Ejaculation'). Good satire exposes small, relatable foibles and magnifies them to comic effect; the piece should allow readers to laugh at themselves while recognizing the truth behind the exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concrete, authentic micro-details
rubrics_metrics.description: The tiny details ring true: names of record stores, guys geeking out on particular songs, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounding satire in recognizable, specific details (place names, niche references, realistic behaviors) makes the exaggeration funnier and more believable. Example: '37 Record-Store Clerks Feared Dead In Yo La Tengo Concert Disaster' succeeds because the small touches make the situation ring true. Anti-pattern: vague or generic phrasing that fails to evoke a lived-in world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of recognizable social archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture and caricature social types so readers see themselves or people they know (e.g., 'Vehement Anti-Cell-Phone Guy Finally Caves', 'Area Man Has Far Greater Knowledge Of Marvel Universe Than Own Family Tree').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong pieces present a distilled, exaggerated social archetype with identifiable traits; staff responses show they often choose pieces because they match a known persona. The value lies in recognizability and specificity rather than obscure in-jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elicits mixed emotional response (humor + discomfort/unease)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful piece can make you laugh and also feel weird or uneasy about how accurately it reflects you: 'I always feel a twinge whenever I see "Ugly Girl Killed," because sometimes I wonder if the Onion people got a picture of me ... I always laugh at and feel weird about that article.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good satire may produce ambivalence: amusement coupled with self-consciousness. This emotional complexity is a sign the piece hit a deep cultural or personal nerve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective use of short-form 'news in brief' structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Concise, news-brief formats (one-paragraph headlines/briefs) can deliver satire sharply and memorably (example: 'Glorious New Tomorrow Postponed Indefinitely').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-form items must be tightly written and economical—every line should contribute to the gag. The article highlights that some of the most memorable Onion pieces are brief news items that encapsulate a larger social critique in a compact package.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical critique of grand narratives / promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Target overarching claims or 'all-encompassing belief systems' and expose their empty promises (e.g., the indefinite postponement of the 'glorious new tomorrow').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pieces that lampoon universal assurances (political, religious, cultural) are valued for their skeptical perspective. Good targets are sweeping narratives that affect many people; the satire gains potency by undercutting certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pop-culture specificity and intertextuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage pop-culture references and intertextual touchstones (The Blind Side, Marvel Universe, Simpsons, Muppets) to anchor jokes and create recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referencing widely known cultural artifacts helps readers immediately understand the target and tone. The article's examples show writers often connect to specific cultural texts to make the satire feel timely and personally relevant. Overreliance on obscure references is an anti-pattern unless the audience is similarly niche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to reflect or change behavior / self-awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Onion pieces have real-world influence on readers' behavior or self-presentation (e.g., kept someone from boasting about not owning a TV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A piece that not only describes behavior but causes readers to reconsider or alter their actions demonstrates cultural impact. This is a high bar: satire that prompts self-editing or increased self-awareness is especially potent.
